transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I… um, I’m not even sure how to start. I guess I’m here because I scared myself. I’m a teacher, and usually I can kind of keep it together for the kids—well, my students, I mean, they notice everything, honestly—but lately on the drive home I’ve caught myself thinking that maybe everyone would be better off without me.

And sometimes at night I think it would just be easier if I didn’t wake up. I don’t want to do anything, I don’t want to act on it, but having those thoughts at all really frightened me.
Did these thoughts and the way you’ve been feeling start after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

Yeah… I think it did start around a particular change. It’s been about… a year and seven months now, I think. Around when I took over the STEM assessment redesign at school, on top of my normal teaching load.

It sounds silly when I say it like that, because it’s just curriculum and spreadsheets and meetings, but there were so many extra pieces—like people needing updates, and everyone having opinions, and I’d be trying to grade after dinner and then remember some rubric thing at midnight. Sorry, I’m getting off track. But yes, that’s when it started, or at least when I really noticed it beginning.
Since this started, have you felt this way most days for more than six months?

Yes… most days, definitely. It’s been going on for about a year and seven months now, since I took over that STEM assessment redesign along with my usual teaching load. I keep thinking, “Oh, it’ll settle after this deadline,” but then there’s another meeting or another set of spreadsheets, and somehow it’s just… kept going.
If that school project were taken off your plate, do you think you would still feel this way?

I don’t know. I keep trying to imagine that, like if someone just took the whole binder and the meetings and all the tracking sheets away, whether I’d sort of… snap back.

Part of me thinks I’d feel lighter, obviously. But I’m not sure it would all just disappear. It’s hard to separate it now, because it’s been tied to my whole routine for so long. Even on weekends or breaks, I catch myself still feeling like something is hanging over me. But then again, teachers are terrible at resting—at least the ones I know. We’ll get a day off and spend it reorganizing cupboards or answering emails we swore we wouldn’t answer.

So… I guess I’m not sure. I think it might help, but I don’t know if it would fix everything.
When you’re away from school responsibilities for a while, do you still feel this low?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, when I’m physically away from school—like not in the building, not doing meetings—it doesn’t always switch off in my head.

But then sometimes I wonder if I’m just bad at being “away,” because I’ll be at home and notice the tote bag with papers in it, or I’ll remember some email I haven’t answered, and then suddenly it’s like I’m back there anyway. My partner says teachers have a weird definition of time off, which is probably true… we had a whole conversation once about how summer “break” is not really a break, and then I started making a list of classroom supplies, which kind of proved the point.

So… I don’t know if I can say clearly. I think I can still feel low even when I’m not actively doing school stuff, but I’m not sure how much of that is because it’s still in the background.
Before this started about a year and seven months ago, had you ever gone through another period in your life when you felt depressed like this?

I… don’t really know. I mean, I’ve had hard stretches before, like during uni when everything felt dramatic and impossible for about five minutes—well, it probably wasn’t five minutes, but you know what I mean. And teaching has never exactly been a calm profession, so there have definitely been times I’ve felt really worn down.

But like this? I’m not sure. I can’t think of another time that stands out clearly in the same way. It’s hard because you look back and everything gets sort of blurry, and I start comparing it to exam periods or family stress or my first year teaching, which was its own little disaster. So… I don’t know if I’d say I had another period like this before.
Even when nothing school-related is happening, do you still feel down?

I’m honestly not sure. I want to say yes, sometimes, but then I start picking apart whether “nothing school-related” ever really happens, because my brain will make something school-related out of almost anything. Like I’ll be watching some completely unrelated programme and suddenly think, “Oh, that would make a good example for Year 10,” and then there I am again.

But if you mean, like, if I’m just sitting there and no one’s emailed me and I’m not planning anything… I think I can still feel low. I just don’t know how cleanly I can separate it out. It’s all a bit tangled.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about lots of different things?

I’m not sure I’d call it “lots of different things,” exactly. I do worry, but then I get stuck trying to decide whether it’s excessive or just… being a person with responsibilities.

Like, I can worry about practical things, and then it sort of spirals into remembering something completely unrelated—like I’ll think about paying a bill and then suddenly I’m wondering whether I replied to someone’s message from three days ago. But I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean.

I haven’t really sat down and thought, “Oh, I’m worrying about everything.” It’s more… bits and pieces, I suppose.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different parts of your life?

I don’t really know if I’d say “many different parts.” I mean, I do worry, but then I start making categories in my head, which is probably not what you’re asking. Work sort of leaks into everything, so it’s hard to tell whether I’m worrying about life in general or just one thing wearing different hats.

Like, I’ll be thinking about something ordinary—shopping, or whether I’ve got clean clothes for tomorrow—and then somehow it becomes connected to school, because I need to remember something for a lesson, or I’ve forgotten to print something, and then I’m off on that track. But I don’t sit there with a list of worries about every area of my life, if that makes sense. I’m not sure I’ve noticed it that way.
During these past year and seven months, have you felt down or low nearly every day?

I don’t know if I can honestly say nearly every day, because then I start thinking, well, what counts as “down”? Like, is it the whole day, or waking up with that sort of grey feeling, or just dipping in and out?

It has been around a lot, I think. But I haven’t been marking it on a calendar or anything. And the “past year and seven months” is such a specific stretch that my brain immediately wants to break it into terms and holidays and exam periods, which probably isn’t helpful. I can say it’s felt frequent, but I’m not sure I could confidently say nearly every single day.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I still do the things sometimes, so from the outside it probably looks like I’m interested. But it doesn’t feel the same.

I used to really look forward to softball, and book club, and messing about in the garden—there was always something to check on, or weed, or decide whether I’d planted too many tomatoes again. And I help with the robotics club at school too, which used to be one of those things that made the week feel a bit brighter.

Now I mostly just… go through the motions. Or I cancel. I’ll tell myself I’m too busy, or that someone else can cover it, but if I’m honest, it’s more that none of it feels enjoyable in the way it used to.
For the past two years, have you felt down or depressed most of the time?

Two years… I’m not sure I can pin it down that neatly. I keep trying to line it up with school years, because that’s how I remember time—autumn term, mock exams, summer holidays—and then it gets a bit muddled.

I have felt low a lot, but “most of the time” over two whole years feels hard to answer. Some stretches blur together, and then there are bits where I was just busy or distracted, or I don’t know if I’d have called it depressed exactly. So… I don’t think I can say for certain.
If the school workload were no longer a problem, do you think you would still feel depressed?

I’m not sure, honestly. Part of me wants to say yes, because the workload is such an obvious thing to blame, isn’t it? Like marking piles up and suddenly everything feels impossible.

But then… I don’t know. Even in lighter weeks, I can’t always tell whether I actually feel better or whether I’m just less cornered. It’s hard to separate it out. Teaching kind of leaks into everything—weekends, evenings, even when I’m buying milk I’m thinking about whether Year 10 understood the lesson.

So if the workload disappeared completely… I don’t know. Maybe I’d feel better. Maybe I’d still feel low and just have fewer excuses for it.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yeah… sleep’s been pretty rubbish, actually. I can be completely exhausted, like barely keeping my eyes open while I’m brushing my teeth, and then as soon as I’m in bed my brain starts doing this awful replay of everything.

It’ll be assessment deadlines, or some tiny mistake I made in class, or whether I handled something badly with a pupil—things that probably no one else is even thinking about. And then I’ll wake up around 4 in the morning and just… lie there. Sometimes I doze a bit, but I don’t really get properly back to sleep.
Have you noticed a clear change in your appetite?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not like I decided to eat less, or anything like that. It’s more that on school days I’ll get to, I don’t know, three or four o’clock and realise I’ve only had coffee or maybe half a cereal bar that was in my bag.

Sometimes I tell myself I’ll eat at break, and then there’s a student at the door, or someone needs the photocopier code, or I’m trying to mark something quickly, and then lunch just sort of… disappears. Our staffroom fridge is also disgusting, which doesn’t help—people leave yoghurts in there for weeks.

But yes, my appetite’s definitely changed. I’m not really trying to lose weight, but over the last year my clothes have got noticeably looser. At first I thought maybe things had stretched in the wash, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but… yeah, it’s enough that I’ve noticed.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yes… quite a lot, actually. It’s embarrassing because teaching is basically being able to make decisions every thirty seconds, isn’t it? And I used to be quick with marking, not necessarily cheerful about it, but quick.

Now I’ll read the same student answer three or four times and still sit there thinking, “What mark is that?” Like I can see the words, but they don’t… settle into meaning properly. And then I start second-guessing the mark scheme, and whether I’m being fair, and whether I’m too harsh on that particular class because they were awful after lunch on Tuesdays—sorry, that’s probably not relevant.

Even simple things can take forever. I had to order lab supplies the other day—just basic stuff—and I got completely stuck choosing what to get. I think I spent nearly an hour going back and forth over it, which is ridiculous. It’s like my brain just won’t move on.
Have you been moving or speaking noticeably more slowly than usual?

Um… I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think anyone’s said I’m speaking slowly or anything.

Moving slowly… I mean, mornings at school can feel like wading through treacle, but that might just be because the photocopier jams every other day and Year 9 always seem to appear before I’ve even taken my coat off. Sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I suppose I haven’t noticed myself being noticeably slower in a way other people would point out. I might feel slow inside, if that makes sense, but I don’t know if I look or sound slower.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or drained of energy?

Yes. By the time I’ve got through a full day of teaching and then, say, a department meeting, I feel completely wrung out. Like my body’s heavy, if that makes sense.

And then I’ll get home and even making dinner feels like this huge thing. Or I’ll open my laptop to answer a few parent emails and it feels like climbing a hill. Which is silly, because it’s just typing, but I just feel so drained.
Has this been making it hard for you to function at work or at home?

Yes. I mean… I’m still going in, so part of me keeps thinking, well, it can’t be that bad, can it? But it is affecting things.

I’m falling behind on marking and lesson planning, and that does spill into the classroom. I hate that. I used to be really meticulous with grades, probably annoyingly so, and recently I made a mistake with one and it really scared me. Not scared like dramatic, just… it felt unlike me, and I kept thinking about the student and whether I’d let them down.

And at home I’m not really… showing up, I suppose. Friends message and I either don’t reply or I say I’m busy, and family things feel like too much. My life has got very small: get through school, come home exhausted, then somehow do it again.
What is the longest stretch of time you've felt depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

The longest stretch… I think it’s been about a year and seven months now. It sort of started when I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my normal teaching load.

I remember thinking at first, “Well, it’s just a busy term,” because in teaching everything gets blamed on the term, doesn’t it? There’s always some deadline or data drop or someone needing a spreadsheet in a slightly different colour. But it didn’t really lift after that. It’s been most days, most of the day, for… yeah, about a year and seven months.

target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about a clear change in appetite, which matches the appetite/weight change symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. It’s not like I decided to eat less, or anything like that. It’s more that on school days I’ll get to, I don’t know, three or four o’clock and realise I’ve only had coffee or maybe half a cereal bar that was in my bag.

Sometimes I tell myself I’ll eat at break, and then there’s a student at the door, or someone needs the photocopier code, or I’m trying to mark something quickly, and then lunch just sort of… disappears. Our staffroom fridge is also disgusting, which doesn’t help—people leave yoghurts in there for weeks.

But yes, my appetite’s definitely changed. I’m not really trying to lose weight, but over the last year my clothes have got noticeably looser. At first I thought maybe things had stretched in the wash, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but… yeah, it’s enough that I’ve noticed.

inference.note: Added F32.2 because there is now clear evidence of a depressive syndrome with suicidal ideation, anhedonia, insomnia, and decreased appetite/weight loss. F34.1 is less supported because duration under 2 years and symptom severity appears beyond dysthymia. Adjustment disorder remains possible given onset with work stressor, though major depressive episode is increasingly favored.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode includes impaired concentration/indecisiveness, which would help confirm major depressive disorder severity and distinguish it from adjustment disorder or generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble concentrating?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: I’ll read the same student response three or four times and still not know what score to give it, and simple choices like which lab supplies to order can stall me for an hour.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about trouble concentrating, which matches diminished ability to think or concentrate.

patient.answer:
Yes… quite a lot, actually. It’s embarrassing because teaching is basically being able to make decisions every thirty seconds, isn’t it? And I used to be quick with marking, not necessarily cheerful about it, but quick.

Now I’ll read the same student answer three or four times and still sit there thinking, “What mark is that?” Like I can see the words, but they don’t… settle into meaning properly. And then I start second-guessing the mark scheme, and whether I’m being fair, and whether I’m too harsh on that particular class because they were awful after lunch on Tuesdays—sorry, that’s probably not relevant.

Even simple things can take forever. I had to order lab supplies the other day—just basic stuff—and I got completely stuck choosing what to get. I think I spent nearly an hour going back and forth over it, which is ridiculous. It’s like my brain just won’t move on.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode is severe by assessing psychomotor retardation or agitation, which helps distinguish F32.2 from milder depressive diagnoses and from adjustment disorder/GAD.
doctor.question: Have you been moving or speaking noticeably more slowly than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor changes, specifically moving or speaking more slowly than usual, but the provided symptom profile does not include a psychomotor agitation/retardation item.

patient.answer:
Um… I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think anyone’s said I’m speaking slowly or anything.

Moving slowly… I mean, mornings at school can feel like wading through treacle, but that might just be because the photocopier jams every other day and Year 9 always seem to appear before I’ve even taken my coat off. Sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I suppose I haven’t noticed myself being noticeably slower in a way other people would point out. I might feel slow inside, if that makes sense, but I don’t know if I look or sound slower.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode meets the severity threshold for major depression by assessing fatigue/loss of energy, which would add another core vegetative symptom and help distinguish severe/unspecified depressive episode from adjustment disorder or generalized anxiety.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually tired or drained of energy?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By the time I get through teaching and a department meeting, my body feels so heavy that even making dinner or answering a few parent emails feels like climbing a hill.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feeling unusually tired or drained of energy, which matches the Fatigue symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes. By the time I’ve got through a full day of teaching and then, say, a department meeting, I feel completely wrung out. Like my body’s heavy, if that makes sense.

And then I’ll get home and even making dinner feels like this huge thing. Or I’ll open my laptop to answer a few parent emails and it feels like climbing a hill. Which is silly, because it’s just typing, but I just feel so drained.

inference.note: Current evidence strongly supports a depressive episode: anhedonia, insomnia, reduced appetite/weight loss, poor concentration, low energy, and passive suicidal ideation. GAD is less supported because worry appears largely work-linked rather than excessive across multiple domains, so F41.1 is dropped. Adjustment disorder remains possible given onset with a stressor, but duration and symptom severity make a depressive disorder more likely.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode includes marked functional impairment, which helps distinguish severe major depressive episode (F32.2) from unspecified depressive episode (F32.9) and from adjustment disorder (F43.2).
doctor.question: Has this been making it hard for you to function at work or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m falling behind on grading and lesson planning in ways that affect my classroom, and the grading mistake scared me because I used to be meticulous. I’ve also stopped showing up for friends and family the way I used to, so most of my life has narrowed to barely getting through school and then going home exhausted.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are making it difficult to function at work or at home, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… I’m still going in, so part of me keeps thinking, well, it can’t be that bad, can it? But it is affecting things.

I’m falling behind on marking and lesson planning, and that does spill into the classroom. I hate that. I used to be really meticulous with grades, probably annoyingly so, and recently I made a mistake with one and it really scared me. Not scared like dramatic, just… it felt unlike me, and I kept thinking about the student and whether I’d let them down.

And at home I’m not really… showing up, I suppose. Friends message and I either don’t reply or I say I’m busy, and family things feel like too much. My life has got very small: get through school, come home exhausted, then somehow do it again.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms represent a major depressive episode rather than an adjustment disorder by establishing the duration of a continuous low-mood period.
doctor.question: What is the longest stretch of time you've felt depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about 1 year and 7 months, since I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my regular teaching load.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the depressed mood has persisted most of the day, nearly every day, which directly matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
The longest stretch… I think it’s been about a year and seven months now. It sort of started when I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my normal teaching load.

I remember thinking at first, “Well, it’s just a busy term,” because in teaching everything gets blamed on the term, doesn’t it? There’s always some deadline or data drop or someone needing a spreadsheet in a slightly different colour. But it didn’t really lift after that. It’s been most days, most of the day, for… yeah, about a year and seven months.

opening_question.intent: Open the interview by learning the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a single prolonged depressive episode lasting about 1 year and 7 months with depressed mood most days, anhedonia, insomnia, reduced appetite with weight loss, impaired concentration, fatigue, suicidal thoughts, and clear functional impairment at work and home. There is no clear evidence of prior distinct depressive episodes, supporting a current single depressive episode rather than recurrent depressive disorder. Although symptoms began in the context of a major work-related stressor, the syndrome is persistent, pervasive, and severe enough to meet criteria for a severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms rather than adjustment disorder.
